newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine seeks more foreign investment in sell-off.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine seeks more foreign investment in sell-off.

text.p: Ukraine plans to increase the number of companies selling shares targeted at foreign investors as it tries to get its privatisation programme moving, a government adviser said on Thursday.

"So far we're seeking foreign investment for 208 companies, but the list eventually will increase," Myron Wasylyk, adviser to the State Property Fund (FDM), the state privatisation agency, told Reuters.
Ukraine, which has been criticised in the past for the slow pace of privatisation, has attracted only about $1.5 billion in foreign investment since independence in 1991.
It is now trying to speed up privatisation.
The government intends to finish the planned sale of 70 percent of shares in around 5,000 companies by the end of the year, it said in a programme submitted to parliament last week.
Stakes of more than 70 percent in over 3,800 of these companies have been sold since 1995, and privatisation of small businesses is nearly complete.
The next stage is to convert some 8,000 large- and medium-size enterprises into joint stock companies for potential share issues, the government programme said.
It also calls for increased foreign investment in privatised companies. Foreign investment is to rise to $1.4 billion a year by 1999 from a forecast $832 million this year.

Under the scheme strategic foreign investors buying shares in selected companies must agree to modernise them and make them profitable within a set period. Eight companies on the list of 208 are already preparing tenders.

The State Property Fund is seeking consulting firms to prepare for tender the sale of 51 percent of AT Poltavsky Zavod Hasorozryadnykh Lamp, a gas lamp factory, and an as-yet undetermined number of shares in the AvtoZAZ carmaker, which recently signed an investment feasibility study with General Motors.

OP Mykolayivsky Hlynozemniy Zavod (MHZ), an alumina plant which supplies many Russian smelters, and shipbuilder AT Sudnobudivny Zavod Okean have announced they are seeking strategic foreign investment money.

Papermaker AT Zhydachivsky Tselulozno Paperovy Zavod, busmaker AT Lvivsky Avtobusny Zavod, the port of Odessa Odesky Pryportovy Zavod, and two steel companies AT Donetsky Metalurhiny Zavod and OP Metalurhiny Kombinat Azovstal will eventually commission consulting firms to prepare investment tenders, Wasylyk said.
The Zhydachivsky paper plant and the Lviv bus factory will each offer 26 percent of their shares to foreign investors.

The State Property Fund has also asked parliament to remove vetoes placed in 1994 and 1995 on the sale of 1,250 of 6,500 strategic enterprises which were part of the military-industrial complex during the Soviet era.
About half of the firms on the moratorium list include agriculture and food enterprises such as grain elevators, fish hatcheries, and wine producers.
Others included oil and gas sector firms, machine builders, chemical producers, and railway servicing companies.

"Many have moved to regular industrial production," said Wasylyk. "We're talking about a boot factory for the army. That's not a military enterprise and has no strategic value to the country, so there is no need to keep (it) in state hands."
The government also wants to complete the issue of privatisation certificates by the end of the year, although parliament says this deadline may be extended.
Each of Ukraine's 52 million people -- adults and children -- is entitled to a certificiate worth about $250 which can be used to buy shares in privatised companies by mid-1997.
About 80 percent of Ukrainians have so far picked up their certificates, which can be sold or pooled, and 45 percent have already started buying shares with them. -- Kiev Newsroom, +380 44 229 2264
